findings.text: The first sentence tells a newcomer what Athena is and what sets it apart: one model does the work, another checks it, and the cost is recorded. This is the strongest part of the page.
findings.source: Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost.

findings.text: The page says why it exists: it shows Athena explaining a project with every statement traced to source lines. A newcomer can tell this is a sample of Athena's output, not Athena's own documentation.
findings.source: Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it with every statement traced to a claim, and every claim to lines in the project's own files.

findings.text: This URL is Athena's home page, but after three short paragraphs the page is entirely about firstmate, a separate project. A newcomer who came to learn about Athena gets one sentence about what Athena does and has to leave the page to learn more.
A link near the top points straight to the next steps, so a newcomer doesn't have to read the dense study to find out what to do.
findings.source: Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself.

findings.text: The install step assumes the reader already has a checkout. The page gives no clone command and no prerequisites (for example a Rust toolchain or AI model access), and it doesn't say what the example `athena ask "add a changelog"` will do or cost.
findings.source: Install Athena from a checkout of its repository: ./setup.sh

findings.text: The "Start here" section and the short list of terms before first use help, and the step-by-step "One piece of work, start to finish" list is clear. But terms like "place", "exit 75", "merge authority" and "guarded fast-forward" still show up before they are explained, so a newcomer has to work hard to follow.
The glossary is honest about a gap, but a definition that admits it defines nothing, given twice, reads as odd to a newcomer. A one-line note would do the job.
findings.source: <dt>in scope</dt><dd>The words firstmate's instructions use for the work that yolo lets firstmate merge itself. The cited instruction does not say what makes work in scope, so this page gives no test for it.</dd>

findings.text: Most of the page is a dense state-machine reference with citation tags on every line. It suits someone checking how firstmate works, but it is heavy going for a newcomer, and the same terms are defined again in the glossary.

The "Limits of this study" section frankly says nothing was run and that a first reading missed several paths. That builds trust, but it may also make a newcomer doubt the very ability the page is meant to show.
